title: Fisher information
dek: I(θ) = E[−∇²ℓ(θ)] = Var(score). It is the expected curvature of the log-likelihood, and the usual large-sample precision of the MLE.
story: The score S(θ) = ∇ℓ is a mean-zero random vector under regularity. Its covariance is Fisher information I(θ). Equivalently I(θ) = E[−∇²ℓ(θ)]: expected curvature. Lots of information means a peaky expected log-likelihood and a tight MLE.

Observed information J(θ̂) = −∇²ℓ(θ̂) is the Hessian you have in hand after the fit. Expected information wants an average over Y, often evaluated at θ̂. Software SE columns are usually √diag(J⁻¹) or √diag(I(θ̂)⁻¹). They are not mystical.

Additivity: independent experiments add information. Two labs with independent isolates give I_total = I₁ + I₂. Dependent reads from the same isolate do not. That is the whole reason phylogenetic and mixed models exist: they stop you from adding information you do not have.
deep: For iid data, I_n(θ) = n I₁(θ), so se(θ̂) ≈ 1/√(n I₁). That is the √n in every delta-method talk. If you change parameterisation, information transforms by a Jacobian: I_φ = I_θ / (dφ/dθ)² in 1-D. Quote SEs on the scale you interpret.

Singular I(θ) means local non-identification: two directions in parameter space the data cannot separate. Classic in over-parameterised mixture models and in some clock-plus-tree phylogenetic likelihoods. A giant SE or a failed inversion is a scientific message.

Cramér–Rao uses I(θ) as a bound for unbiased estimators. Asymptotic efficiency of the MLE is the statement that √n (θ̂ − θ) →d N(0, I₁⁻¹). Both fail on boundaries and for non-iid likelihoods you have not written.
In a Bernoulli experiment I₁(π) = 1/(π(1−π)). Information is smallest near 0 and 1 — rare resistance alleles are poorly estimated not because the lab is careless but because the curvature vanishes.

example.title: Information for a Poisson rate
example.setup: Yᵢ iid Poisson(λ), n = 9, ȳ = 2. Compute I(λ) and the model-based SE of λ̂ = ȳ.

steps.title: One-observation information
steps.body: ℓ₁ = y log λ − λ. Score y/λ − 1. −∂²ℓ₁/∂λ² = y/λ², so I₁(λ) = E[Y]/λ² = 1/λ.

steps.title: Sample of n
steps.body: I_n(λ) = n/λ. At λ̂ = 2, se ≈ √(λ̂/n) = √(2/9) ≈ 0.47. Same as Var(ȳ) = λ/n.

steps.title: Reparameterise
steps.body: If φ = log λ, I₁(φ) = λ = e^φ. SE on the log scale is 1/√(nλ) ≈ 0.24. A Wald interval on φ, then exponentiated, is often better behaved than λ̂ ± 1.96×0.47 when λ is small.

example.takeaway: I(θ) is expected curvature. Invert it on the scale you will interpret, or transform with the delta method.

check.prompt: Independent experiments add Fisher information. Dependent observations from the same isolate:
choices: Also add I as if they were independent
Do not add a full I each; the joint likelihood must carry the dependence
Force observed and expected information to coincide
check.answer: Do not add a full I each; the joint likelihood must carry the dependence
check.why: Additivity of I is additivity of independent scores. Shared isolates, trees, and labs break that.

whyWrong.Have zero information: They have information, just not n times I₁.

check.prompt: iid Bernoulli, n = 50, π = 0.2. Expected information I_n(π) equals:

whyWrong.0.16: That is π(1−π), the variance of one Y, not information.

check.prompt: On the information plate, the “ridge” in the full box is warning you about:
check.figureHint: Full model lists θ₂ ≈ a + b θ₁ and singular I.
choices: A well-identified MLE with tiny SEs
A direction in parameter space the likelihood does not curve, so I is nearly singular
The χ² reference of an LRT
check.answer: A direction in parameter space the likelihood does not curve, so I is nearly singular
check.why: Non-identification is flatness. Inverting I then explodes or fails — which is the correct alarm.

whyWrong.The χ² reference of an LRT: Different object, though nested LRTs also fail when I is singular under H₀.
